entries.title: Berkshire textile control: cheap price, weak business
entries.summary: Buffett later identified taking control of the struggling textile business as a major early mistake. A low purchase price could not fix poor long-term economics; the company ultimately became a capital-allocation vehicle rather than a textile success.
entries.evidence: His 1989 shareholder letter explicitly revisits the 1965 purchase and describes the limits of buying superficially cheap businesses.
entries.interpretation: The lesson is that expected future returns on reinvested capital can overwhelm an apparent discount to asset value.
entries.limitations: This retrospective lesson is not a claim that every asset-discount investment is unsuccessful.
entries.locator: Mistakes of the First Twenty-five Years

entries.title: National Indemnity: pivoting toward insurance
entries.summary: Berkshire entered property-casualty insurance by acquiring National Indemnity and National Fire and Marine Insurance in 1967 for approximately $8.6 million. By 1977 Berkshire described significant growth in the insurance group.
entries.evidence: The 1977 shareholder letter gives the year, businesses, original purchase price and underwriting economics.
entries.interpretation: Insurance float, if conservatively underwritten and managed, gave Berkshire capital for other investments.
entries.limitations: The letter also records underwriting mistakes and cyclicality; float is not inherently free.

entries.title: See’s Candies: buying an economic franchise
entries.summary: Blue Chip Stamps bought control of See’s in January 1972. Buffett reported that the sellers ultimately accepted a $25 million price; his subsequent discussions emphasized See’s high returns on modest tangible capital and its ability to price a trusted product.
entries.evidence: The 1991 letter details the negotiating price and the 1983 letter explains economic goodwill using the same business.
entries.interpretation: The acquisition illustrates why a brand with enduring earning power can be more valuable than its factories and inventories.
entries.limitations: It is a historical acquisition, not evidence that today's confectionery companies have identical economics.
entries.locator: Twenty Years in a Candy Store; Goodwill and its Amortization

entries.title: GEICO during distress: an investigated franchise
entries.summary: Following serious underwriting and pricing errors at GEICO, Buffett describes Berkshire buying a large stake during the second half of 1976. By year-end 1980 Berkshire had invested $45.7 million and held roughly one-third of shares.
entries.evidence: The 1995 shareholder letter describes the turnaround under Jack Byrne, the investment amounts, and Buffett’s long familiarity with the insurer.
entries.interpretation: A potentially durable low-cost business can survive solvable distress, but only after understanding its liabilities and management changes.
entries.limitations: The case cannot be reduced to buying any distressed insurer or assuming every crisis is temporary.

entries.title: Nebraska Furniture Mart: cost advantage and stewardship
entries.summary: Berkshire purchased 90% of Nebraska Furniture Mart in 1983. Buffett credited Rose Blumkin and her family's purchasing, low operating costs and customer value proposition rather than a financial-engineering thesis.
entries.evidence: The 1983 shareholder letter explains the 90% interest and the store's cost discipline and management story.
entries.interpretation: An operational cost advantage and trusted manager can be more compelling than a superficially cheap stock.
entries.limitations: The primary letter contains contemporary claims about store competitiveness, not an audited forever-moat.

entries.title: Coca-Cola: a consumer franchise purchased late
entries.summary: Berkshire began buying Coca-Cola in 1988 and increased its stake in 1989. The 1989 letter reported roughly $1.024 billion cumulative cost at that year-end and associated the business's appeal with global reach, marketing and management execution.
entries.evidence: Buffett wrote about observing Coca-Cola as a consumer product decades before purchasing its shares; the 1989 holdings table reports shares and cost.
entries.interpretation: A patient investor can still change his opportunity set as business quality becomes clearer; having used a product is not sufficient due diligence.
entries.limitations: This is a retrospective explanation of the period, not a current fair-value or price recommendation.

entries.title: Gillette: structured convertible preferred investment
entries.summary: In 1989 Berkshire purchased $600 million of Gillette convertible preferred stock, paying an 8.75% dividend with a mandatory ten-year redemption and conversion terms.
entries.evidence: The 1989 shareholder letter provides the amount, security type and dividend terms.
entries.interpretation: The structure illustrates how terms and contractual cash flows can materially affect an investment thesis beyond the brand.
entries.limitations: Do not treat a preferred-stock crisis instrument as equivalent to buying ordinary shares at the same date.

entries.title: USAir: a reminder to examine security terms
entries.summary: Berkshire purchased $358 million of USAir convertible preferred stock in 1989 with a 9.25% dividend and specified conversion rights.
entries.evidence: The 1989 letter states the amount and terms of the USAir preferred purchase.
entries.interpretation: This is a useful contrast to consumer franchises: securities with high contractual coupons still involve business and industry risk.
entries.limitations: The source alone does not establish whether Buffett ultimately made or lost money on this position.

entries.title: Salomon: reputational risk and active oversight
entries.summary: In 1991 Buffett became interim chairman of Salomon amid serious difficulties at the company. He discussed the additional oversight burden in Berkshire's 1991 letter.
entries.evidence: The 1991 shareholder letter records his interim-chairman role and its contrast with his normally decentralized work.
entries.interpretation: Owning a security sometimes means taking responsibility for governance risks, not merely modeling cash flows.
entries.limitations: Detailed causal or legal conclusions should be checked in contemporaneous filings; this note is not a complete history of the episode.

entries.title: Dexter Shoe: the share-issuance error
entries.summary: Buffett described Berkshire's 1993 Dexter Shoe purchase for $434 million as a particularly severe mistake. He used Berkshire shares; by year-end 2016 those shares had become worth over $6 billion while Dexter's value had gone to zero.
entries.evidence: Buffett gives the cost and retrospective share dilution in the 2016 shareholder letter.
entries.interpretation: The cost of an acquisition includes the future upside surrendered by issuing shares, not just the accounting purchase price.
entries.limitations: The $6 billion share figure is a 2016 retrospective comparison, not a modern fair value for Dexter.
entries.locator: What We Hope to Accomplish, p. 4

entries.title: GEICO: completing ownership for $2.3 billion
entries.summary: In 1995 Berkshire agreed to pay $2.3 billion to acquire the roughly 50% of GEICO it did not already own. The deal closed shortly after year-end. Buffett tied the purchase to GEICO's longstanding cost position and management.
entries.evidence: The 1995 letter explains the price, ownership change and his association with GEICO since the early 1950s.
entries.interpretation: A long familiarity with a business and strong operator can justify a negotiated full-business purchase when management believes the price sensible.
entries.limitations: Buffett explicitly called the price steep; this is not proof that paying any premium is prudent.

entries.title: General Re: an acquisition with a costly share payment
entries.summary: Berkshire announced its approximately $22 billion General Re merger in 1998. Buffett later called using Berkshire stock for the deal a major mistake, despite valuing General Re as an operating business.
entries.evidence: The 1998 company announcement states the consideration; the 2016 letter discusses the 272,200 shares issued and retrospective dilution.
entries.interpretation: Business quality and financing choice are two separate questions: shareholders can overpay with an undervalued currency.
entries.limitations: This is Buffett's later assessment of the share exchange, not a claim that the acquired insurer never had value.

entries.title: MidAmerican Energy: diversification into utilities
entries.summary: Buffett's 2016 retrospective describes Berkshire purchasing 76% of MidAmerican Energy in early 2000 for cash, helping develop its collection of controlled non-insurance businesses.
entries.evidence: The 2016 shareholder letter explains the stake, the use of cash rather than Berkshire stock and later strategic consequences.
entries.interpretation: Capital allocation can favor dependable long-lived infrastructure over liquidity when the purchase economics and managers are sound.
entries.limitations: This account does not provide a complete valuation or regulatory risk analysis of a utility.
entries.locator: What We Hope to Accomplish, p. 4

entries.title: Goldman Sachs: structured capital during the crisis
entries.summary: In 2008 Goldman Sachs agreed to sell Berkshire $5 billion of cumulative preferred stock with a 10% dividend plus warrants to acquire common shares at $115 per share, subject to the documented terms.
entries.evidence: Goldman's SEC Form 8-K and announcement specify the preferred security, size, coupon and warrant.
entries.interpretation: Analyze financing and downside protection at the instrument level; a headline investment is not necessarily a plain common-stock bet.
entries.limitations: The filings establish transaction terms, not an exhaustive account of Buffett's private decision process.

entries.title: BNSF: acquiring the railroad for a long-term thesis
entries.summary: Berkshire and BNSF announced in November 2009 that Berkshire would pay $100 per share in cash and stock for the remaining 77.4% of the railroad it did not own. The release valued the transaction at about $44 billion including BNSF debt.
entries.evidence: The contemporaneous announcement in SEC exhibits gives the stake, terms, total transaction value and Buffett's statement connecting rail transport to U.S. economic development.
entries.interpretation: This is an asset-intensive, long-horizon capital allocation bet rather than a simple high-margin consumer franchise purchase.
entries.limitations: The cited document records the signed announcement; it should not be used alone to infer closing date or subsequent performance.

entries.title: Buffett's 2024 letter: acknowledging judgment errors
entries.summary: The 2024 reporting-year letter discusses errors in appraising future business economics and management, and the importance of correcting mistakes rather than overlooking them.
entries.evidence: The first pages of the official 2024 shareholder letter have an explicit section on errors at Berkshire.
entries.interpretation: An evidence-driven knowledge base should preserve negative cases as prominently as successes.
entries.limitations: This is a thematic retrospective; it does not identify the company or size of every mistake.
entries.locator: Mistakes — Yes, We Make Them at Berkshire, p. 1

entries.title: Treat shareholders as long-term owner-partners
entries.summary: Berkshire's Owner's Manual frames shares as fractional interests in a business and explains how managers and shareholders should think of themselves as partners.
entries.evidence: The 1996 manual states the owner-partnership operating principles.
entries.interpretation: Research the economics of ownership, not only price quotations or short-term relative performance.
entries.limitations: This is Berkshire's stated governance philosophy, not a binding promise of investment success.

entries.title: Measure progress by intrinsic value per share
entries.summary: The Owner's Manual places long-term improvement in per-share intrinsic business value above increases in corporate size or annual headline reported profit.
entries.evidence: The manual's third owner-related principle describes the per-share goal.
entries.interpretation: When assessing acquisitions, reinvestment or buybacks, examine whether the decision plausibly improves per-share economics.
entries.limitations: Intrinsic value is an estimate, not an observable accounting line.

entries.title: Compare buying entire businesses with owning minority stakes
entries.summary: Berkshire states a preference for owning whole cash-generative businesses where terms make sense, while also purchasing parts of attractive businesses via public securities.
entries.evidence: The manual's fourth principle describes both capital allocation routes.
entries.interpretation: The opportunity cost of buying a company is what the same capital could earn through other investments.
entries.limitations: No rule says whole ownership is always preferable at any price.

entries.title: Economic goodwill is not the same as accounting goodwill
entries.summary: Buffett's 1983 letter contrasts intangible franchise value with book accounting and uses See's Candies to illustrate earnings generated on small tangible capital.
entries.evidence: The appendix explains returns on net tangible assets, accounting amortization and consumer franchise economics.
entries.interpretation: A company able to raise prices without continually adding capital may be valuable well beyond recorded net assets.
entries.limitations: Not every recognizable brand is a moat; goodwill recorded in acquisitions can also reflect overpayment.
entries.locator: Goodwill and its Amortization: The Rules and The Realities

entries.title: Test pricing power and capital intensity together
entries.summary: The See's example distinguishes price-setting power and favorable consumer experience from sheer asset accumulation.
entries.evidence: Buffett's 1983 economic-goodwill discussion describes these mechanisms.
entries.interpretation: Investigate whether unit economics and free cash flow withstand inflation and competitor responses.
entries.limitations: Historical brand strength does not prove future pricing power, nor does a single margin observation.

entries.title: Choose industries with economic tailwinds
entries.summary: The 1977 letter compares the difficulties of textile manufacturing with the more resilient outcomes of the insurance activities, while admitting insurance underwriting errors.
entries.evidence: The shareholder letter directly contrasts sector economics and management effort.
entries.interpretation: A difficult industry can limit the returns of even excellent management.
entries.limitations: Insurance is cyclical and can experience severe losses; the lesson is not that all insurers are structurally attractive.

entries.title: Insurance float requires underwriting discipline
entries.summary: Buffett describes policyholder funds available for investment and explains that underwriting losses can make their funding expensive.
entries.evidence: The 1986 letter discusses combined ratios, reserve uncertainty and the insurance group's sources of advantage.
entries.interpretation: A good investing outcome requires both sound underwriting and responsible investing of funds subject to claims.
entries.limitations: Float is not debt-free profit; catastrophe risk, liabilities and duration mismatches matter.

entries.title: Understand the business behind GAAP totals
entries.summary: The 1988 letter criticizes treating consolidated numbers as a complete picture of a diversified company's economic value and obligations.
entries.evidence: Buffett discusses supplementary segment reporting and limitations of conventional accounting.
entries.interpretation: Focus on operating segments, liabilities and economic returns, with accounting reports as evidence rather than the conclusion.
entries.limitations: Adjusted analysis must remain transparent and reconcile to audited figures.

entries.title: Intrinsic value is a forward-looking cash-flow estimate
entries.summary: The 1989 letter explains that rational business valuation discounts future cash inflows and outflows, while acknowledging limitations of forecasting.
entries.evidence: The letter explicitly introduces future cash-flow discounting when distinguishing intrinsic value from book value.
entries.interpretation: Use assumptions and sensitivity ranges, not false precision or a claim of an observable objectively correct number.
entries.limitations: A DCF remains uncertain even when every spreadsheet formula is mathematically correct.

entries.title: A low purchase multiple does not rescue a poor enterprise
entries.summary: Reflecting on his own purchases, Buffett distinguishes a short-term bargain liquidation from holding a business that earns too little for years.
entries.evidence: His 1989 letter includes a section describing what went wrong with the cigar-butt approach.
entries.interpretation: Prefer identifying durable earning power and the future return on reinvestment over relying solely on historical asset discounts.
entries.limitations: The discussion is not a blanket rejection of all distressed or asset-based investing.
entries.locator: Mistakes of the First Twenty-five Years

entries.title: Every acquisition competes with other uses of capital
entries.summary: Berkshire describes comparing a negotiated business purchase with passive interests in public businesses, rather than acquiring simply to meet a growth target.
entries.evidence: The 1995 letter contrasts discretionary acquisition discipline with a rigid strategic plan.
entries.interpretation: Reject projects that are inferior to the next-best alternative after risk and price are considered.
entries.limitations: The comparison needs contemporaneous prices and realistic future assumptions.

entries.title: Select outstanding managers and avoid unnecessary interference
entries.summary: The 1995 letter connects Berkshire's decentralized structure with management integrity, operational ability and shareholder-oriented incentives.
entries.evidence: Buffett describes excellent managers and the small size of Berkshire headquarters.
entries.interpretation: Strong incentives and judgment at operating subsidiaries can reduce head-office complexity.
entries.limitations: Decentralization does not eliminate fraud, oversight failures or governance duties.

entries.title: Treat seller projections with skepticism
entries.summary: Buffett criticizes optimistic projections prepared by sellers and their advisers in acquisitions.
entries.evidence: The 1995 letter's acquisitions section discusses asymmetric information and buyer incentives.
entries.interpretation: Use independent downside cases and evidence from actual operations rather than treating promotional forecasts as guaranteed cash flows.
entries.limitations: Forecasting remains necessary in valuation; skepticism is not proof that every seller estimate is inaccurate.

entries.title: A share represents business ownership, not price movement
entries.summary: The Owner's Manual discusses seeing shares as long-held ownership interests and evaluating business outcomes rather than short-term fluctuations.
entries.evidence: Buffett's manual describes the owner model and long holding periods.
entries.interpretation: Build a research thesis from customer economics and capital allocation before considering market volatility.
entries.limitations: Quoted price still matters when entering, exiting or reallocating positions.

entries.title: Account for taxes and the cost of unnecessary turnover
entries.summary: Buffett explains that selling appreciated shares can trigger tax liabilities and diminish the compounding advantage of long ownership.
entries.evidence: The 1989 letter models the deferred-tax burden on the owner's position.
entries.interpretation: Compare after-tax outcomes rather than treating every portfolio switch as frictionless.
entries.limitations: Actual tax consequences depend on jurisdiction, account type and current law.

entries.title: Guard against the institutional imperative
entries.summary: Buffett identifies organizational pressures that foster expansion, imitation and flattering forecasts even when economics do not support them.
entries.evidence: The 1989 mistakes discussion describes typical institutional behaviors.
entries.interpretation: Challenge managerial incentives and social conformity rather than equating activity with value creation.
entries.limitations: Organizational dynamics are a risk to investigate, not a claim of misconduct at any specific company.

entries.title: Scale changes the opportunity set
entries.summary: Berkshire's 1991 letter explains that as its capital base grew, small successful investments could no longer move overall results meaningfully.
entries.evidence: The letter compares contributions to return on a small versus a much larger equity base.
entries.interpretation: A strategy that worked for a small partnership may be impractical for a giant conglomerate.
entries.limitations: This is a constraint on deployable opportunity size, not a statement that all big funds underperform.

entries.title: Stock re-rating and business earnings are different
entries.summary: Buffett notes that Coca-Cola and Gillette gains in 1991 reflected both genuine earnings growth and rising valuation multiples, cautioning that the latter cannot recur indefinitely.
entries.evidence: The opening of his 1991 letter separates earnings progress from a market reappraisal.
entries.interpretation: Don't extrapolate a period of multiple expansion as though it were a recurring operational growth rate.
entries.limitations: A rising multiple can be rational, but should not be confused with business cash-flow growth.

entries.title: Paying with stock has an intrinsic economic cost
entries.summary: Buffett's 2016 review of Dexter Shoe and General Re emphasizes the amount of Berkshire's future value given away through stock issuance.
entries.evidence: The 2016 letter provides a detailed retrospective on both acquisitions and dilution.
entries.interpretation: Evaluate the intrinsic value of the currency used to buy a business, not only the nominal deal price.
entries.limitations: This does not imply all stock-for-stock acquisitions destroy value.
entries.locator: What We Hope to Accomplish, p. 4

entries.title: Retained earnings must earn their keep
entries.summary: The 2016 letter connects Berkshire's retention of substantial earnings with the responsibility to reinvest capital productively over time.
entries.evidence: Buffett discusses normalized earning power and stewardship of retained shareholder capital.
entries.interpretation: Judge growth by incremental economics and per-share owner returns, not size alone.
entries.limitations: The right reinvestment rate depends on available projects and their uncertainty.

entries.title: Build capacity to act when unusual opportunities appear
entries.summary: Buffett describes preparing financially to deploy capital during extraordinary periods of distress rather than assuming opportunities arrive predictably.
entries.evidence: His 2016 letter discusses the need for capital and willingness to act during infrequent downturns.
entries.interpretation: Liquidity and disciplined readiness can have option value, but idle cash has an opportunity cost.
entries.limitations: This is not a market-timing signal or prediction of the next crisis.

entries.title: Operating subsidiaries and public shares are different forms of ownership
entries.summary: The 2022 letter distinguishes full control of subsidiaries from passive ownership of publicly traded companies.
entries.evidence: The shareholder letter's introductory section separates managerial roles in the two ownership modes.
entries.interpretation: Research decision rights and information access when comparing a controlled acquisition to a minority public stock investment.
entries.limitations: The economics of each holding still depend on valuation and operating performance.

entries.title: Admit mistakes and correct them
entries.summary: In the 2024 letter Buffett discusses mistakes assessing business futures and managers and criticizes delaying corrective action.
entries.evidence: The opening portion of the 2024 reporting-year letter contains the explicit mistakes discussion.
entries.interpretation: A serious investing system needs disconfirming evidence, not just victory stories.
entries.limitations: Retrospective honesty does not retroactively remove shareholder losses.
entries.locator: Mistakes — Yes, We Make Them at Berkshire, p. 1

entries.title: The Intelligent Investor — Benjamin Graham
entries.summary: Benjamin Graham authored The Intelligent Investor, first published in 1949. It is a foundational text in value investing, associated with discipline, securities analysis and the margin-of-safety tradition. Graham was Buffett's teacher, as Buffett recounts in his 1995 letter.
entries.evidence: The publisher/editor's catalog identifies Graham and the original book; Buffett's 1995 letter describes studying under him.
entries.interpretation: Use the book as an influence on Buffett's thinking, and compare that early approach with Buffett's later discussion of economic goodwill.
entries.limitations: Not written by Buffett; the book's text remains copyrighted and is neither embedded nor reproduced.
entries.locator: Publisher catalog; GEICO Corporation in 1995 letter

entries.title: The Essays of Warren Buffett — edited by Lawrence Cunningham
entries.summary: Lawrence Cunningham organized and edited Buffett's shareholder writings into thematic essays, initially for a 1997 symposium and later book editions. This is a curated interpretation and compilation rather than an additional stream of previously unknown letters.
entries.evidence: Cunningham's George Washington University entry documents editorial authorship and the original symposium.
entries.interpretation: Use it to orient reading by governance, finance, acquisitions and accounting themes, then consult the primary letters.
entries.limitations: Do not treat the edited book as an open license to redistribute original Buffett text.

entries.title: The Snowball — Alice Schroeder
entries.summary: Alice Schroeder's Buffett biography draws on her access to Buffett and associates and adds biographical context to his investing choices.
entries.evidence: Penguin Random House identifies Schroeder as author and describes the collaboration and sources.
entries.interpretation: Biographical stories are useful context, but test specific investment facts against contemporaneous letters and filings.
entries.limitations: This is a third-party biography, not Buffett's own memoir; no portion is rehosted here.

entries.title: Poor Charlie's Almanack — Charlie Munger
entries.summary: This anthology is centered on Charlie Munger's talks and mental models, edited by Peter D. Kaufman. Munger influenced Berkshire's investment approach, but his ideas must be attributed to him, not silently to Buffett.
entries.evidence: Stripe Press identifies Munger as speaker and Kaufman as editor.
entries.interpretation: Cross-disciplinary mental models can complement an evidence-led business analysis without replacing financial verification.
entries.limitations: This is not a Buffett-authored book and its copyrighted contents are not embedded.

entries.title: Annual-meeting Q&A archive: watch the primary recording
entries.summary: CNBC hosts the licensed archive of Berkshire Hathaway annual meetings from 1994 onward, including searchable transcripts, interview material and subject-oriented video clips.
entries.evidence: CNBC describes the provenance and features of the authorized recording archive.
entries.interpretation: For a question about what Buffett said in a specific year, find the original meeting, exact speaker and context rather than relying on quote collections.
entries.limitations: We link to the licensed archive; videos and transcripts are not copied into the open-source project.

entries.title: 1994 annual meeting: reinsurance and derivative risk
entries.summary: CNBC's official page for the 1994 annual meeting describes Buffett warning that excessive reinsurance risks may emerge only years later and discussing derivatives and leverage.
entries.evidence: The CNBC meeting summary supplies the date, subjects and its original video archive.
entries.interpretation: The value of this source is a dated first-hand discussion: verify any quotation at the linked recording instead of reconstructing his words from memory.
entries.limitations: This note paraphrases CNBC's summary and does not quote or redistribute the recording.

entries.title: Scott Fetzer: why Berkshire paid above book value
entries.summary: Berkshire paid $315.2 million for Scott Fetzer in early 1986 versus its $172.6 million book value. In the 1994 shareholder letter Buffett detailed how after-tax business earnings grew while book value barely increased.
entries.evidence: Berkshire's 1994 shareholder letter includes the original purchase price, acquisition-year net assets and a nine-year earnings and dividends table.
entries.interpretation: The case shows the difference between accounting purchase-premium amortization and the business's actual cash economics under manager Ralph Schey.
entries.limitations: The 1994 report is a retrospective, not a complete model of what the property would sell for today.
entries.locator: 1994 letter, Book Value and Intrinsic Value

entries.title: Helzberg's Diamond Shops: management was part of the deal
entries.summary: Berkshire acquired Helzberg's in 1995 after Barnett Helzberg Jr. approached Buffett in 1994. Buffett wrote that he would not have purchased the retailer without confidence in its manager, Jeff Comment.
entries.evidence: The 1995 letter reports the approach by Helzberg, the 1995 stock-exchange closing, 134 stores by the time of the initial discussion and management's role.
entries.interpretation: When judging an acquisition, investigate operator quality and incentives alongside economics, not simply the store count or reported growth.
entries.limitations: Berkshire's assessment of the manager was its contemporaneous judgment; it is not universal proof that all successful retailers rely on identical management traits.

entries.title: R.C. Willey: acquiring a leading retailer with durable execution
entries.summary: Berkshire acquired furniture retailer R.C. Willey in 1995 after an introduction through the Nebraska Furniture Mart managers. The 1995 letter reports $257 million of annual sales and describes intensive competition in retail.
entries.evidence: The 1995 shareholder letter details the referral, valuation exchange, mid-year merger, and the competitive risks Buffett believed the business faced.
entries.interpretation: The example illustrates that understanding the management team and daily retail execution can matter as much as an established regional market position.
entries.limitations: The sales figure is historical; a regional share of furniture spending does not constitute a permanent defensive moat.

entries.title: FlightSafety International: Berkshire uses its stock in an acquisition
entries.summary: Berkshire's 1996 letter documents that it issued a combination of Class A and Class B shares as part of the FlightSafety International acquisition.
entries.evidence: The letter's opening financial reconciliation identifies the FlightSafety transaction as a reason Berkshire share count and per-share book value differed from aggregate growth.
entries.interpretation: A transaction must be evaluated for the value of ownership surrendered by existing shareholders as well as the acquired operating asset.
entries.limitations: The letter excerpt establishes the mode of financing, not a full historical business valuation or realized return.

entries.title: Circle of competence: knowing the boundary matters
entries.summary: Buffett's 1996 shareholder letter emphasizes that investors do not need expertise in every company, only the ability to evaluate selected businesses within areas they understand.
entries.evidence: The 1996 shareholder letter directly contrasts broad market knowledge with the limited set of enterprises an investor can appraise competently.
entries.interpretation: Decline to form a confident valuation where industry economics, accounting or competitive factors are outside the researcher's knowledge.
entries.limitations: This principle does not mean less-understood companies are inherently poor businesses or investments.

entries.title: Macro forecasts should not dominate business appraisal
entries.summary: Buffett's 1994 shareholder letter lists historical geopolitical and market surprises and argues that concentrating on durable business economics avoids the need to forecast them accurately.
entries.evidence: The letter's opening paragraphs identify many unexpected events and state that Berkshire continued evaluating businesses on fundamentals.
entries.interpretation: Investment analysis should explicitly stress-test uncertainty without pretending it can predict the exact course of macroeconomic headlines.
entries.limitations: Macro factors still influence discount rates, capital availability, employment, demand and liquidity; ignoring all such exposures is not warranted.

entries.title: In his own words: forward valuation
entries.summary: When Berkshire's securities had risen relative to intrinsic value by 1989, Buffett contrasted past performance with the harder work of assessing what returns remained possible.
entries.evidence: This exact short excerpt appears in the opening valuation discussion of the official 1989 Berkshire shareholder letter.
entries.interpretation: Historical return figures alone cannot establish intrinsic value or expected returns from current prices.
entries.limitations: The original discussion addresses 1989 Berkshire investments and is not a prediction about today's market.
entries.locator: 1989 letter, opening discussion of intrinsic versus book value
entries.verbatimExcerpt: The rear-view mirror is one thing; the windshield is another.
entries.speaker: Warren E. Buffett

entries.title: In his own words: scale
entries.summary: Buffett described how Berkshire's much larger capital base shrank its feasible opportunity set in 1994, creating a structural disadvantage versus its smaller past.
entries.evidence: This short excerpt appears in the opening discussion of capital scale in Berkshire's 1994 shareholder letter.
entries.interpretation: An investment can be very attractive for a small account but too small to influence a vast portfolio.
entries.limitations: The claim is about opportunity size and Berkshire's constraints at the time, not proof that every large fund must underperform.
entries.locator: 1994 letter, opening discussion of investment universe
entries.verbatimExcerpt: A fat wallet, however, is the enemy of superior investment results.
entries.speaker: Warren E. Buffett

entries.title: In his own words: valuation discipline
entries.summary: Buffett acknowledged the substantial price for purchasing the remaining interest in GEICO in the 1995 letter instead of depicting the transaction as an automatic bargain.
entries.evidence: The exact sentence follows his disclosure of the $2.3 billion agreement to acquire the portion of GEICO Berkshire did not already own.
entries.interpretation: A high purchase price can coexist with a credible quality thesis, but must be evaluated on the actual deal terms.
entries.limitations: These words alone do not establish the value of GEICO today or guarantee Berkshire's subsequent return.
entries.speaker: Warren E. Buffett

entries.title: In his own words: circle of competence
entries.summary: Buffett urged investors to concentrate on businesses they can evaluate rather than trying to acquire superficial expertise in every market sector.
entries.evidence: This exact short passage occurs in the 1996 letter's discussion of the investor's circle of competence.
entries.interpretation: A research process should reward explicitly declining unanswerable questions rather than manufacturing confidence.
entries.limitations: Circle-of-competence judgments are investor-dependent and cannot be determined by a financial ratio.
entries.verbatimExcerpt: The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital.
entries.speaker: Warren E. Buffett
